claims.current_activity: providing armoured support during the Juno landings
claims.notes: Brigade-level (below stated scope; included for context). An independent armoured brigade, not an organic part of the 3rd Canadian Division: Wikipedia lists it among the independent brigades and says it was assigned to British Second Army in January 1944, and it landed on 6 June with the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division, under its command for the assault (Wikipedia; Veterans Affairs Canada names the division and the brigade together as the designated assault formations). Its regiments were usually tasked individually to infantry units. 1st Hussars attacked Le Mesnil-Patry 11 June. [Review: parent_unit_id stays the 3rd Canadian Division (operational parent, now relationship attached); organic parent is now Second Army (was the 3rd Canadian Division); current_activity reworded from 'landing at Juno Beach in support of 3rd Canadian Division'; confidence raised from 0.5 to 0.7 by the rubric (approximate location, two source families: Wikipedia and Veterans Affairs Canada). Wikipedia's First Canadian Army page says the division and brigade were detached from that army to British I Corps for the assault; that standing link is not modelled because the army was not in Normandy on this date.]

claims.current_activity: lands on Gold Beach near Hable de Heurtot as the right-flank reserve brigade of the 50th Division
claims.notes: Event date: 6 June 1944, about noon (Ellis, vol. I, p. 178: about an hour after the 151st Brigade began landing at about eleven). Event definition: The brigade, the second reserve brigade of the 50th Division in the Gold assault, starts landing about noon near Hable de Heurtot instead of on Jig beach, to avoid fire from le Hamel (Ellis, p. 178); by the night its leading troops have passed la Rosière and turned south astride the Bayeux road, the South Wales Borderers securing the Aure bridge at Vaux-sur-Aure (p. 210). Wikipedia says the brigade formed the right flank of the 50th Division on Gold Beach. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, pp. 178-179: "About an hour later the 56th Brigade started landing near Hable de Heurtot so as to avoid fire from le Hamel"; pp. 210-211: "Leading troops of the 56th Brigade had also passed through la Rosiére and turned southwards astride the road to Bayeux"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "where it formed the right flank of the 50th (Northumbrian) Infantry Division on Gold Beach". Location: Gold Beach (PL0156) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the Gold Beach sector; the landing place, Hable de Heurtot, and the night positions inland are not separate places in the dataset. Location support: Ellis names Hable de Heurtot on the Gold beaches (p. 178); Wikipedia names Gold Beach. Context: Relationship: attached to the 50th Division from the landing (Wikipedia: attached to the 50th Division until 10 June); XXX Corps as the 50th Division's corps, with the row date as start (inferred value).

Event definition: With the 7th Armoured Division's attack stalled, two tank-infantry groups are formed on 11 June; the first, under command of the brigade, renews the attack on Tilly-sur-Seulles and fights into the middle of the town by evening, but the tanks fail to get round the flank and the group is withdrawn when it grows dark (Ellis, p. 252). On the afternoon of 12 June, when the 7th Armoured Division moves off with its own lorried brigade, the brigade reverts to the 50th Division (p. 254). Wikipedia says all its battalions were involved in the taking of Tilly-sur-Seulles. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 252: "the first, under command of 56th Infantry Brigade to renew the attack on Tilly sur Seulles"; "At Tilly the 56th fought their way into the middle of the town by the evening"; p. 254: "the 56th Brigade reverted to the 50th Division"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "It remained attached to the 50th Division until 10 June, after which it was attached to the 7th Armoured Division until 12 June". Location: Tilly-sur-Seulles (PL0349) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the town, which the brigade fought into; it was withdrawn at dark. Location support: Ellis names the town (p. 252). Context: Relationship: the 7th Armoured Division attachment is dated by the sources, 11 to 12 June (Ellis pp. 252 and 254; Wikipedia gives from 10 June); the earlier attachment to the 50th Division is closed the day before (inferred value).

claims.notes: Event date: 11 June 1944, 1 p.m. (Stacey, p. 139; Ellis, vol. I, p. 253). Event definition: Ordered to clear the Mue valley, the brigade attacks on 11 June at very short notice, the orders having reached it only that morning; the 6th Armoured Regiment (1st Hussars), with the Queen's Own Rifles riding on its tanks, passes through Norrey-en-Bessin and deploys in the cornfields north of Le Mesnil-Patry under fire, and the attack fails with heavy loss (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 252-253; Stacey, p. 139). Wikipedia calls the battle a partial success with severe losses. Event support: three source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Stacey, the Canadian official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 253: "Unfortunately orders did not reach the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade and their associates The Queen's Own Rifles till the morning of the 11th"; "they deployed in the open cornfields north of le Mesnil Patry"; Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 139: "Planning begun on 10 June for an enterprise by the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade south of Norrey-en-Bessin"; Wikipedia, 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade: "the Battle of Le Mesnil-Patry on 11 June 1944, ended with only a partial success and severe losses to the Canadians". Location: Le Mesnil-Patry (PL0221) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the village, the objective; the fighting was in the fields north of it. Location support: Ellis, Stacey and Wikipedia name Le Mesnil-Patry. Commander: Brigadier R. A. Wyman (Stacey, pp. 139 and 216), wounded on 8 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 237). Context: Relationship: under the 3rd Canadian Division (existing relation from D-Day) and I Corps as that division's corps, start = row date (inferred value). claims.current_activity: capturing Cherbourg and its port
claims.notes: VII Corps captured Cherbourg (Schlieben surrendered 26 June, deputy Sattler 27 June; arsenal/harbour forts 29 June). Port heavily demolished. [Review (V-006): references added for the 21st Army Group relationship (CR0166). R445 (US Army in WWII, The Supreme Command, ch. 15) says that although the 12th Army Group became active on the Continent on 1 August and Montgomery channeled his orders to the U.S. armies through it, the 21 Army Group commander retained over-all control until 1 September. R007 (Wikipedia, 21st Army Group) says that on 1 September 1944 the group was relieved of operational control of the American armies. These sources disagree; CR0166 ends on 31 July (12th Army Group operational, 1 August) and CR0116 records the August coordination; these two sources date the end of 21st Army Group control a month later. The dates are left unchanged pending a decision (see docs/review/verification_results.md, V-006).]

claims.notes: Panzer IVs of 21st Panzer supported Kampfgruppe Frey (1st SS Panzergrenadier Regiment, placed under 12th SS Panzer) north of the Odon on 28 June toward Mouen and Tourville (Wikipedia, Epsom). Saunders, Operation Epsom (via erenow): the tanks were 4 Kompanie, Panzer Regiment 22, with five operational Mark IVs in action; Frey's grenadiers and tanks overwhelmed C Company 3rd Monmouthshire (159th Brigade, 11th Armoured Division) with 3rd County of London Yeomanry tanks at Mouen, attacked Colleville in the late morning (held by 2nd Glasgow Highlanders of 15th Scottish Division) and were driven back by local counter-attacks, and 10th Highland Light Infantry (227th Brigade, 15th Scottish) with a squadron of tanks counter-attacked Mouen at 19:45. Wikipedia: Frey gained Mouen and British counter-attacks supported by tanks halted any further advance but could not retake it. Only a company-sized element of the division is documented that day; the row records that element's part in one connected action (Mouen/Tourville attack, Colleville thrust, evening British counter-attack), not a division-wide operation. It is kept as one row because the sources give no separate place or opponent for the pieces. claims.current_activity: arriving on the Continent
claims.notes: Event date: CMH ETO-OB chronology: arrived on the Continent 13 July 1944. Event definition: arrival of the division on the Continent as CMH records it, with the command post at the vicinity of Mesnil-St-Martin, Manche, listed on this date (CMH gives the CP only as a vicinity of the town). Wikipedia and USHMM give 11 July for the Utah Beach landing (row C0243): the rows describe two events, the landing and the arrival, which may be different phases of the landing. Location caveat: the CMH CP name "Mesnil-St-Martin" could not be resolved to a Manche commune with certainty. The Nominatim match used before (about 49.0, -1.29, near Percy) lies roughly 50 km from the landing beaches and is inconsistent with the later CP at Méautis (17-18 July) and with a unit that had just landed at Utah Beach (Coutances was not taken until 28 July); the point is therefore unreliable and is kept only as a very wide inferred point. The unit was in the Cotentin beachhead assembly area (a 37th Tank Battalion report puts the division assembly area in use on 12 July). [Review (open item 7, 26 October 2026): conflict group G012 was re-read against the sources available. The CMH ETO-OB chronology has the division "arrived Continent 13 July" with the command post at Mesnil-St-Martin on 13 July (and at Dorchester, England on 8 July); Wikipedia and USHMM have the landing at Utah Beach on 11 July; the Breakout and Pursuit volume (ch. 7 p. 132) calls it "the newly arrived 4th Armored Division" when it relieved the 4th Division after 15 July and gives no landing date; the dday-overlord.com order of battle repeats the CMH command-post list and adds no date of its own. No source read says the two dates are the same event or that either is wrong, and none dates the main body ashore. The two rows are therefore kept as separate events and not as rival claims: no source read says the two dates are the same event or that either is wrong, and the event types differ (landing, arrival). Decided by Scott on 26 October 2026, no date, place or confidence changed: conflict group G012 is dissolved. Before, C0243 had claim_status alternate and C0244 preferred, both with conflict_group_id G012; now both rows are preferred and have no conflict group. The rows describe two events, the first landing at Utah Beach on 11 July (USHMM, Wikipedia) and the arrival with the command post at Mesnil-St-Martin on 13 July (CMH ETO-OB), and the sources do not contradict each other.]

claims.current_activity: LXXXIV Corps falls back to the Lessay-Périers line in the night of 13/14 July with Kluge's authorization
claims.notes: Event date: Breakout and Pursuit ch. 7 p. 128: "Kluge on 13 July authorized the corps to fall back to the south banks of the two rivers. The withdrawal begun that evening was gradual and orderly"; the Lexikon der Wehrmacht LXXXIV. Armee-Korps page has Choltitz ordering a withdrawal behind the Lessay sector in the night to 14 July; Schramm, OKW war diary (p. 325): on 11 July Hitler approved the request of OB West to fall back to the line from the southwest edge of the Prairies Marécageuses to Angoville, and put off the request to go back to the line Confreville-Saint-Germain. Event definition: the withdrawal of the night of 13/14 July; the 11 July row in Schramm is the approval of a shorter line in the Cotentin, the CMH and the Lexikon give the order and the evening of 13 July; the three sources do not name the same line, so the event is the withdrawal, not one line. Location: the Lessay-Périers line; the point is the midpoint of the two dataset places, with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the CMH names the line of Lessay and Périers (ch. 7 p. 128); the midpoint is a representative point of the line. Location support: good: three source families agree that the corps withdrew on the night of 13/14 July. Commander: Generalleutnant Dietrich von Choltitz; the Lexikon commander list has him from 17 June to 30 July (its narrative has 20 July, so the dates inside the Lexikon differ). Relationship: the corps stays under the Seventh Army (CR0006).

Fallschirmjäger-Division (Masse), 17. SS-Panzergrenadier-Division, Schnelle Brigade 30, 2. SS-Panzer-Division, Gruppe König (77th, 91st, Kampfgruppe 265th), 353rd (Masse), 243rd (Masse) and the 319th. Event definition: the division is a member of the corps order of battle on 15 July; this supports July over June, but does not date the start of the subordination. Juni 1944", do not name Panzer Lehr, which makes the June reading of C0790 unlikely; Breakout and Pursuit ch. 7 p. 128 (R591) has Choltitz, the LXXXIV Corps commander, out of reserves by 12 July and the Panzer Lehr commander threatening to leave with his tanks, before Kluge let the corps fall back on 13 July, which puts the division in that corps' sector by 12 to 13 July; and the existing relations keep it under the I SS Panzer Corps to 10 July (CR0043) and under the Seventh Army from 11 July (CR0578). The start of the subordination therefore lies between 10 and 15 July, and this dated list is the best-supported row; C0791 (month-level, one family) and C0790 (June) become alternates. Search of 26 October 2026 (open item 7, G012): the IGN geocoder (data.geopf.fr, address and place-name layers) has no commune or place called Mesnil-Saint-Martin or Le Mesnil-Saint-Martin in Manche (the nearest names are Le Mesnil-Aumont in Saint-Martin-de-Cenilly, 48.99 N 1.29 W, and Le Mesnil-Rouxelin near Saint-Lo, neither identified with the CMH command post); the point is kept as the wide inferred point it was (precision 50 km).
claims.current_activity: arriving on the Continent
claims.notes: CMH ETO-OB chronology: arrived on the Continent 18 July 1944. Location is the nearest listed CP at Le-Mesnil-St-Martin, Manche (CMH ETO-OB), 1 days after the row date; the division position on the day is not stated. Location caveat: the CMH CP name "Mesnil-St-Martin" could not be resolved to a Manche commune with certainty. The Nominatim match used before (about 49.0, -1.29, near Percy) lies roughly 50 km from the landing beaches and is inconsistent with the later CP at Méautis (17-18 July) and with a unit that had just landed at Utah Beach (Coutances was not taken until 28 July); the point is therefore unreliable and is kept only as a very wide inferred point. The unit was in the Cotentin beachhead assembly area (a 37th Tank Battalion report puts the division assembly area in use on 12 July).

claims.current_activity: Goodwood: Second Army attacks with VIII Corps in the centre, I Corps on the left and II Canadian Corps on the right
claims.notes: Event date: 18 July 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 336, 340). Event definition: General Dempsey's orders for 18 July: I Corps is to establish the 3rd Division on the east flank, VIII Corps is to establish its three armoured divisions in the Vimont, Garcelles-Secqueville and Hubert-Folie-Verrieres areas, and II Canadian Corps is to take Giberville and Vaucelles; troops of all three corps are engaged from the morning of 18 July (pp. 336 and 340). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 336: "Put shortly General Dempsey's orders to his corps commanders for July the 18th were as follows"; p. 340: "Though troops of all three corps were engaged simultaneously". Location: Orne bridgehead / east of Caen (existing place PL0265) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the bridgehead east of the Orne from which the attack started; it is not the Army headquarters. Location support: Ellis places the attack in the bridgehead east of the Orne (p. 335); the Army headquarters place is not stated. Commander: General Dempsey, the Second Army commander (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 336 and 386).

claims.current_activity: Goodwood: the three armoured divisions of VIII Corps lead the advance south from the bridgehead east of the Orne
claims.notes: Event date: 18 July 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 335, 336). Event definition: VIII Corps strikes south between I Corps and II Canadian Corps with the Guards, 7th and 11th Armoured Divisions: its orders are to establish the divisions in the areas of Vimont, Garcelles-Secqueville and Hubert-Folie and Verrieres so firmly that no enemy can penetrate between them; the three divisions cross the Orne one after another and cannot enter the battle together (p. 335). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 336: "VIII Corps, in the centre, was first to get the main bodies of its armoured divisions so firmly established in the areas of (a) Vimont, (b) Garcelles-Secqueville and (c) Hubert-Folie and Verriéres that there could be no enemy penetration between them, and enemy armour brought against them would be defeated"; p. 335: "the three armoured divisions of VIII Corps which were to lead the advance". Location: Cagny, Calvados (existing place PL0529) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is Cagny, in the middle of the corps objectives; none of the three areas is the corps headquarters. Location support: Ellis names the three areas but no single corps position; Cagny is the village fought over by the corps in the centre of that front (pp. 341-343). Commander: General O'Connor, VIII Corps (Ellis, vol. I, p. 394).

claims.notes: Event date: 18 July 1944 (Stacey, pp. 171 and 173: "the morning of the 18th"; Ellis, vol. I, p. 343). claims.notes: Event date: 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 408). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 408: "Its first effect was on Second Army"; "By the evening of the 4th the left was at the Orne near Amaye, the centre had reached Evrecy". Location: Evrecy, Calvados (place added in the July tranche) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Evrecy, the centre of the corps line on the evening; the corps headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Evrecy as the place reached by the centre of the corps (p. 408). Review (clean-up 2, 29 October 2026; place merge): the old place_id is PL0724 (Evrecy, Calvados), the new place_id is PL0527; the reason is that both rows are the same place (data/place_merges.csv). The coordinates are unchanged and now carry a coord_override, because the survivor point (Wikipedia) is about 100 m away. Review (clean-up 2 follow-up, 29 October 2026; precision): the old precision_km is 5, the new precision_km is 10; the reason is that the row is a corps front, not a single position, so the corps sector rule of 10 km applies; the point Ellis names is kept, and the place, date and confidence are unchanged.

claims.current_activity: under the 59th Division, reaches the Orne upstream of Grimbosq
claims.notes: Event date: 5 August 1944, nightfall (Ellis, vol. I, p. 408). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. Commander: Brig. W. S. Clarke, commander from June 1943 (Wikipedia, 34th Armoured Brigade).

claims.current_activity: under the 59th Division, follows the German withdrawal to the Orne upstream of Grimbosq, near Thury-Harcourt
claims.notes: Event date: 5 August 1944, nightfall (Ellis, vol. I, p. 408). Event definition: In the German withdrawal before XII Corps, by nightfall on 5 August the 59th Division, with the 34th Tank Brigade and the brigade under command, has reached the Orne upstream of the 53rd Division; from the loop in the Orne near Thury-Harcourt the British line bends back westwards (Ellis, p. 408). Wikipedia says the brigade came under the 59th Division in early August and lists the liberation of Thury-Harcourt. Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and Wikipedia). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 408: "the 59th Division (with 34th Tank Brigade and 56th Infantry Brigade under command) had reached the river further upstream"; Wikipedia, 56th Infantry Brigade (United Kingdom): "came under command of the 59th (Staffordshire) Infantry Division in early August 1944"; "the liberation of Thury-Harcourt in the Suisse Normande". Location: Thury-Harcourt (PL0347) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town at the Orne loop; the division's front on the river is not located more closely. Location support: Ellis names the Orne loop near Thury-Harcourt (p. 408).

claims.current_activity: Canadian Scottish take Point 168 north of Falaise in a costly afternoon attack; 7th Brigade on Point 159 next day
claims.notes: Event date: 15 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 249). Event definition: On the second day of the advance towards Falaise the 1st Canadian Scottish Regiment, under the 2nd Armoured Brigade, takes Point 168 east of the Falaise road with its heaviest casualties of the campaign so far; on 16 August the 7th Brigade is on the high ground about Point 159 (p. 250). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 249: "On the ridge immediately east of the Falaise Road the 1st Battalion Canadian Scottish Regiment, fighting under command of the 2nd Armoured Brigade, and supported by the 1st Hussars, met and beat down tenacious opposition on Point 168"; p. 250: "Meanwhile the 3rd Division had pushed south from Point 168 and the 7th Brigade occupied the high ground about Point 159"; p. 248: "On the morning of the 15th our advance towards Falaise was resumed". Location: Falaise, Calvados (north of the town) with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: Point 168 is a map height a few miles north of Falaise; the point is the town of Falaise and stands for the area, with a wider precision. Location support: Stacey names Point 168, a height east of the Falaise road, and does not give a village; Point 159 is described as the southern butt of the ridge above Versainville (p. 249). Commander: Brig. J. M. Blackader, the 8th Brigade commander, who took the division temporarily after Keller was wounded on 8 August (Stacey, pp. 224 and 230). Activity: in_line, span point, inferred; in the activity rollout, Canada and France (October 2026), the old value of activity_status is blank, the new value is in_line (point, inferred); reason: the cited source describes part of the division (a brigade, battalion, combat command, column, patrol or advance detachment) in action on this date; the main body is taken to be in the line with it, so the value is inferred.

claims.current_activity: Tractable: switched to the left flank, reaches the Dives at Jort and forces a crossing
claims.notes: Event date: 15 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 250; Ellis, vol. I, p. 431, the day after the bombing of 14 August). Event definition: Switched across to the left flank of the corps, the division reaches the River Dives at Jort on 15 August and forces a way over it; on 16 August it is ordered to cross there and move south-east on Trun parallel to the 4th Canadian Armoured Division. Event support: two source families (Stacey, the Canadian official history and Ellis, the British official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 250: "the Poles, advancing farther north, were to cross the Dives at Jort (which they had reached on the 15th)"; Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 431: "The Polish division had meantime been switched across to the left flank and there it forced a way over the Dives at Jort". Location: Jort, Calvados (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: both histories name Jort as the Dives crossing reached (Stacey p. 250; Ellis p. 431). Location caveat: Ellis gives no date in the sentence; the day follows from his account of the bombing on the previous day (14 August), and Stacey dates the arrival to the 15th. Commander: Maj.-Gen. S. Maczek commands the division (Stacey, pp. 256, 364 and 561 name General Maczek as its commander; index p. 746). claims.current_activity: Dragoon: parachute and glider landings round Le Muy; drop badly scattered by fog; blocking the Argens valley
claims.notes: Event date: 15 August 1944, from about 0430 (Clarke and Smith, ch. 6, pp. 100-101). Event definition: The task force drops before first light on 15 August round Le Muy to block German movement into the beach area along the Argens corridor; fog scatters the drop, but except for Le Muy itself it executes its D-day missions (Clarke and Smith, chs. 5-6). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 5, p. 77: "The 1st Airborne Task Force's main mission was to prevent German movements into the beach area from the direction of Le Muy and Le Luc through the Argens River corridor"; Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 6, p. 104: "However, except for the seizure of Le Muy, the 1st Airborne Task Force had executed its D-day missions"; Wikipedia, 1st Airborne Task Force: "They were to land around the village of Le Muy". Location: Le Muy, Var (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Le Muy; the drop and landing zones lay round it, and many troopers landed far outside them. Location support: Clarke and Smith and Wikipedia name Le Muy as the drop area. Commander: Major General Robert T. Frederick (Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 3).

claims.current_activity: parachute drop west of Le Muy; no trooper lands on the assigned zones, battalions scattered from Trans to Lorgues
claims.notes: Event date: 15 August 1944, about 0435 (Clarke and Smith, ch. 6, p. 101). Event definition: None of the combat team lands on its drop zones, centred two miles west of Le Muy; the 1st Battalion is scattered from Trans-en-Provence to Lorgues, much of the 2nd lands near La Motte, the 3rd far to the north-east; most of the 1st and 2nd Battalions reach their assembly areas after dawn (Clarke and Smith, ch. 6). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 6, p. 101: "None of the troopers of the 517th Parachute regimental combat team landed on their assigned drop zones"; Wikipedia, 1st Airborne Task Force: "The U.S. 517th PRCT were assigned an area of narrow fields about two miles west of Le Muy". Location: Le Muy, Var (new place) with a precision of 10 km. claims.current_activity: Model takes over Army Group B (and OB West) from Kluge
claims.notes: Event date: Wikipedia's Army Group B page lists Model as commander from 17 August 1944 (Hausser acting 15 to 17 August) and its OB West page lists Model as acting commander from 17 August. The CMH Green Book (Breakout and Pursuit ch. 27 p. 532, 535, row of G018) puts the assumption of command at midnight after 18 August. The sources do not agree and neither is judged better, so both rows are disputed. Event support: the event itself is stated in the cited text (see Event date); only the headquarters place is a representative point. Location support fallback: the point is La Roche-Guyon, the headquarters of claims C0011 and C0202, used as a representative point. Review (German Batch 2 follow-up, 27 October 2026; notes and references only, no value changed): the Lexikon der Wehrmacht (Heeresgruppe B, "Generalfeldmarschall Walter Model 17. August 1944 - Kapitulation") and the Bundesarchiv listing RH 19-IX on the EHRI portal ("17.8.1944: Generalfeldmarschall Walter Model") also date Model's command of Army Group B from 17 August; they are one source family with the Tessin-based Wikipedia list, so the 17 August side of group G018 has one family and the CMH (midnight after 18 August, p. 535) the other. Schramm p. 465 and CMH p. 531 date his arrival at the headquarters to 17 August, a different event from taking over command (see C0933). The group stays disputed with no winner; confidence stays 0.3 because the place is a representative fallback point. Nothing in the dataset says that Model's command ended on 14 September: that date of the old task text is the move to Oosterbeek (see C0934); Army Group B was dissolved on 17 April 1945 (see C0937).

claims.current_activity: passing from Third Army to First Army control at 0600
claims.notes: Event date: Breakout-28 p578: at 0600 on 24 August XV Corps passed from the control of Third Army to that of First Army; Hodges told Haislip to clear the zone for British Second Army elements and to move the 5th Armored south. Event definition: control of the corps moves from Third Army to First Army; the row records First Army operational control. Relationship: First Army operational control from 0600 on 24 August is documented and ends on 29 August (C0503). Third Army assigned is inferred continuity (see the relationship note): Lorraine ch. IV says the corps was taken from Third Army and later returned, the Third Army After Action Report says it was released to First Army, and Wikipedia's subordination table shows First Army only for 24-28 August (secondary), so no source documents a retained Third Army assignment. Location: the CMH command-post list (World War II by Day) has the corps at Mantes-la-Jolie on 20 and on 28 August and no entry between. The Mantes vicinity is inferred from those two entries; it is not claimed that the headquarters stayed there without moving, and on 24 August it may have been elsewhere in the area. The row uses the 20 August entry (four days earlier; 28 August is four days later). Event support: high (Green Book, dated to the hour). Location support: low (command post listed four days earlier).

claims.current_activity: Opens fire across the Seine at Vernon; a battalion and a half of the 43rd Division cross by stormboat during the night
claims.notes: Event date: 25 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 466). Event definition: On 25 August the guns and mortars of XXX Corps open fire across the Seine from Vernon and, fifteen minutes later, the first troops of the 43rd Division cross in stormboats; seven of eight boats are lost, but a battalion and a half cross during the night and sappers bridge the river, a light bridge being completed by the late afternoon of 26 August (p. 466). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 466: "August the 25th, guns and mortars of XXX Corps opened fire on the enemy positions across the Seine from Vernon"; "a battalion and a half crossed during the night". Location: Vernon, Eure (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Vernon as the crossing place of the corps (p. 466). Commander: Lt.-Gen. B. G. Horrocks, who succeeded Lt.-Gen. G. C. Bucknall in command of XXX Corps on 4 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 400; named again on pp. 453 and 469).

claims.current_activity: handing the Mantes bridgehead to XIX Corps and moving for Third Army
claims.notes: Event date: Breakout-31 p672: at noon on 29 August XIX Corps took command of the three divisions in the Mantes bridgehead as the XV Corps headquarters started for an assembly area southeast of Paris and eventual Third Army assignment; the CMH list shows Saint-Léger-en-Yvelines on 29 August and Rozay-en-Brie on 30 August. Event definition: XV Corps gives up the Mantes bridgehead; First Army operational control ends and Third Army control resumes. Relationship: First Army operational control carries an explicit end on 29 August (the hour is not documented, only that the headquarters left at noon); Third Army operational control is restored from 29 August (Third Army After Action Report; Lorraine ch. IV) and the standing assignment during these days is inferred, as in C0502. Third Army 'assigned' is not re-listed because no source uses that word for 29 August. Location: Saint-Léger commune centroid, a stop on the move. Event support: high (Green Book, noon 29 August; Third Army After Action Report). Location support: moderate (CMH list, same day).

claims.current_activity: returning to XIX Corps control in the Mantes bridgehead
claims.notes: Event date: Breakout-31 p672 (noon, 29 August: XIX Corps took command of the 79th, 30th and 2nd Armored Divisions in the bridgehead and moved the 2nd Armored to the lead) and the CMH assignment table (XIX Corps from 29 August). Event definition: division returns to XIX Corps; same date for the narrative and the table, which resolves the apparent 19 August vs 29 August conflict (two different assignments, see C0229 and the 19 August row). Location: bridgehead sector, not the division command post. Relationship: corps and army entries from the CMH table. Breakout-31 p672 says XIX Corps took command of the three divisions at noon on 29 August; the table gives XIX Corps only as the corps (single column), so the link stays unspecified_subordination. The preceding XV Corps command of the division is temporary operational control (C0510). Event support: high (Green Book, noon 29 August, and the table). Location support: low (bridgehead sector).

claims.current_activity: Second Army's drive to the Somme starts from the Vernon bridgehead with two armoured brigade groups of XXX Corps
claims.notes: Event date: 29 August 1944, first light (Ellis, vol. I, p. 468). Event definition: At first light on 29 August two armoured brigade groups, spearheads of XXX Corps, start from the Vernon bridgehead in heavy rain and mist on the first stage of the Army's drive through north-eastern France into Belgium, with the task of forcing the Somme on both sides of Amiens and establishing two armoured divisions in the Amiens-St. Pol-Arras area; XII Corps is to start from Les Andelys the next morning (pp. 468-469). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 468: "At first light on the 29th two armoured brigade groups, screened by armoured cars, started out from the Vernon bridgehead in heavy rain and thick mist". Location: Vernon, Eure (new place) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is Vernon, the bridgehead where the leading elements started; it is not the Army headquarters. Location support: Ellis names the Vernon bridgehead as the start line (p. 468); the Army headquarters is not named. Commander: General Dempsey, the Second Army commander (Ellis, vol. I, pp. 336 and 386). Review (clean-up 2 follow-up, 29 October 2026; precision): the old precision_km is 5, the new precision_km is 10; the reason is that the row is a army front, not a single position, so the army sector rule of 10 km applies; the point Ellis names is kept, and the place, date and confidence are unchanged.

claims.current_activity: built round the 3rd Battalion, 157th Infantry, secures Loriol at the Drôme crossing
claims.notes: Event date: 29 August 1944, afternoon (Clarke and Smith, ch. 9). Event definition: Repulsed at Loriol on 28 August, the task force, now built round the 3rd Battalion of the 157th Infantry, attacks again and secures Loriol in the afternoon of the 29th, but cannot push on to the Rhône (Clarke and Smith, ch. 9). Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). Clarke and Smith, Riviera to the Rhine, ch. 9, p. 166: "despite stiff German opposition, Task Force Butler secured". Location: Loriol-sur-Drôme, Drôme (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Clarke and Smith name Loriol. Commander: Brigadier General Frederick B. Butler, VI Corps deputy commander (Clarke and Smith, ch. 5).

claims.current_activity: After Toulon the division goes up the Rhone valley and reaches Lyon
claims.notes: Event date: 3 September 1944 (Wikipedia; CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 181). Event definition: Landed in Provence on 15 August, the division fights at Toulon, sends reconnaissance squadrons to Montpellier and goes up the Rhone, reaching Lyon on 3 September. Event support: three source families (Wikipedia, the US Army official history (CMH) and de Lattre's History of the French First Army). Wikipedia, 1st Free French Division, section 1944: "With First Army, the division disembarked in Provence on 15 August 1944 and participated in the Battle of Toulon, then went up the Rhône"; "Lyon was reached on 3 September"; CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 10 p. 181: "In the west, French units of the 1st Infantry Division, after overcoming scattered German roadblocks and their own logistical problems, had entered Lyon earlier, on the 3d, and also found the Germans long gone"; de Lattre, The History of the French First Army (1952) p. 128: "the division penetrated Lyons on the 3rd September at eight in the morning". Location: Lyon, Palais de la Foire (east bank of the Rhône), Rhône with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is an existing point in Lyon; the sources give only the city. Location support: Wikipedia and the CMH history both name Lyon and 3 September for the division: two source families for a city-level place (precision 10 km), so 0.7. French follow-up: confidence raised from 0.5 to 0.7 after the CMH history (p. 181) was read as a second source family. Commander: General Diego Brosset commands the division until his death on 20 November 1944 (Wikipedia). French follow-up (de Lattre): de Lattre (p. 128) has the 1st DFL (Brosset) enter Lyon at 08.00 on 3 September, the 36th US Division halting to let it in; a third source family that confirms the day; the place is still the city (precision 10 km), so confidence stays 0.7. Activity: in_line, span point, stated; in the activity rollout, Canada and France (October 2026), the old value of activity_status is blank, the new value is in_line (point, stated); reason: the cited source has the division advancing against the enemy, which is line service.

claims.current_activity: arriving on the Continent
claims.notes: Event date: 7 September 1944 is kept: the CMH command and staff table dates every command appointment to 7 September, CMH lists the CP at the Valognes staging area on that date, and the division history (EUCMH, from the division record) says the division landed at Cherbourg and Utah Beach on 7 September as the first convoy direct from the United States. The CMH chronology table gives "Arrived Continent (D+105)", 19 September 1944 (D+105 is 19 September, so the figure is internally consistent): it appears to be a separate CMH event definition, probably the date the division closed in the staging area, and is not corroborated elsewhere. Location: Valognes is the CMH-listed staging area; the commune centroid is used. The EUCMH history says the division established its headquarters at Bourg de Lestre in the staging area, so the headquarters may have been a few kilometres east of Valognes. The staging-area coordinates are not independently verified. Relationship: the CMH table does not distinguish assigned from attached.

claims.current_activity: Battle of Dompaire: the Langlade combat command destroys the 112th Panzer Brigade
claims.notes: Event date: 13 September 1944 (CMH The Lorraine Campaign, pp. 185, 199; Wikipedia). Event definition: Having joined the XV Corps on 8 September, the division advances east; its combat command L (Colonel de Langlade), after seizing Vittel on 12 September, attacks the German 112th Panzer Brigade at Dompaire on 13 September and destroys it. Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH) and Wikipedia). CMH The Lorraine Campaign ch. 4 p. 185: "On 8 September the 2d French Armored Division, leaving the scenes of its triumphal entry into Paris"; "joined the XV Corps and took over the sector between Montargis and the Marne River"; p. 199: "After seizing Vittel on 12 September, CCL, 2d French Armored Division, continued east and laagered that night just short of Dompaire and Damas"; Wikipedia, 2nd Armored Division (France), section Alsace and Lorraine: "On 13 September 1944 at the town of Dompaire 'Groupement Langlade' destroyed the German 112th Panzer Brigade". Location: Dompaire, Vosges with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the place of combat command L; the rest of the division is to the southwest. Location support: both sources place the battle at Dompaire; the point is the place of one combat command, the rest of the division being echeloned back to the southwest (p. 203), so confidence 0.7. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497; Wikipedia).

claims.current_activity: Panther column is destroyed around Dompaire by the French CCL and US fighter-bombers
claims.notes: Event date: 13 September 1944 (Cole, ch. 4; Wikipedia). Event definition: On 13 September the French CCL (2nd Armored Division) and fighter-bombers drive the Panthers into a killing ground in the valley at Dompaire; in the afternoon seven Mark IVs of the south column are destroyed near Ville-sur-Illon; the brigade becomes little more than a cipher (Cole, ch. 4; Wikipedia, Battle of Dompaire). Event support: two source families (the US Army official history (CMH), and Wikipedia). Cole, The Lorraine Campaign, ch. 4, p. 195: "committed the 112th Panzer Brigade against the XV Corps, with such disastrous results as to make that panzer brigade little more than a cipher in future operational plans"; Wikipedia, Battle of Dompaire: "The inexperienced 112 Panzer Brigade suffered from a series of ambushes by French armoured units with American air support". Location: Dompaire, Vosges with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Cole and Wikipedia name Dompaire. Commander: Colonel Horst von Usedom (Wikipedia, Battle of Dompaire). Opponents: French 2nd Armored Division (Groupement Langlade, CCL); US 406th Fighter-Bomber Group.

Relationship: tactical control passed from AFHQ to SHAEF at 0001B on 15 September, so SHAEF is the operational parent (operational_control); AFHQ retained responsibility for supply, administrative functions and civil affairs within the area overrun pending further developments (G-3 report); that is a theater and territorial responsibility, not a stated administrative control of the army group, so AFHQ is listed with relationship unknown (Batch 2 review; the earlier administrative_control entry was withdrawn). claims.current_activity: passing from AFHQ to 6th Army Group control
claims.notes: Event date: Breakout-32 p701 (6th Army Group operational 15 September with Seventh Army and French First Army); the order reached the headquarters on the afternoon of 14 September, effective 0001B 15 September (6th Army Group G-3 report, ordered_date and effective_from). Event definition: Seventh Army passes from AFHQ to 6th Army Group command; tactical control of the group passed from AFHQ to SHAEF at the same time. Relationship: 6th Army Group assigned from 0001B, 15 September. AFHQ is listed with relationship unknown: the source says AFHQ kept supply, administrative and civil-affairs responsibility 'within the area overrun', which is a theater function and territory, not a statement that AFHQ held administrative control of Seventh Army; the earlier administrative_control entry was withdrawn in Batch 2 corrections. Location: Seventh Army headquarters on this date is not documented in the sources used (a SHAEF message of 9 September only expected it north of Lyon, FRUS 1944 Quebec, doc. 150); the Vesoul point is a representative point in the sector where VI Corps was operating, not a headquarters, and is why confidence is 0.3. Search: the 6th Army Group G-3 report (Lyon, 9-15 September) covers the army group only; the CMH list (World War II by Day) has Seventh Army first at Épinal on 2 October 1944; Breakout-32 p701 and Wikipedia name no place. Event support: high (6th Army Group report, order of 14 September). Location support: very low (representative point, headquarters not located).

Location support: Ellis and Stacey name Dunkirk. Commander: Brigadier B. W. Leicester, R.M., commander since the Normandy landings (Ellis, vol. II, p. 118; Stacey, p. 412). claims.current_activity: drives to Douarnenez and takes the surrender of an isolated group of 300 Germans

claims.notes: Event date: 16 October 1944 (Siegfried p305: at 1544 on 16 October the 1st Division chief of staff reported troops of the 18th Infantry on Ravels Hill seeing the 30th Division men at Würselen; p312: the juncture closed the Würselen gap in the Aachen encirclement). Event definition: XIX Corps is credited with the northern arm of the encirclement of Aachen: its 30th Division, after piercing the West Wall near Palenberg, meets VII Corps' 1st Division. Location: Corps command post at Heerlen from 13 October (atlas); no move is recorded for 16 October, so the nearest earlier entry is used. Coordinates: Wikipedia (en): Heerlen. Event support: high (a timed telephone call in the Green Book). Location support: moderate (atlas list entry three days before; the corps place is a town centroid). Commander: the Green Book names McLain as the XIX Corps commander (p401, p499).

claims.current_activity: Under the First French Army and its II Corps, the division pushes south from the Selestat region
claims.notes: Event date: 15 December 1944 (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 486: the planned start of the II Corps push); transfer to the First French Army effective 5 December (p. 464). Event definition: Passed to the operational control of the First French Army on 5 December and attached to the II Corps, the division pushes south from the Selestat region between the Rhine and the Ill from 15 December; on 28 December Devers returns it to the Seventh Army. Event support: one source family (the US Army official history (CMH)). CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 26 p. 464: "the 6th Army Group commander decided to transfer operational control of the U.S. 36th Infantry Division and the French 2d Armored Division from the Seventh to the First French Army, effective 5 December"; p. 486: "de Monsabert's II Corps, with the U.S. 36th Infantry and the French 2d Armored Divisions attached, would push south from the Selestat region on the 15th"; p. 488: "Between the Rhine and the Ill rivers, Leclerc's armor had difficulty penetrating the canal-laced, water-soaked Alsatian plains without more infantry"; CMH Riviera to the Rhine ch. 27 p. 496: "Instead he transferred Leclerc's 2d Armored Division from the First French Army to the American Seventh to further beef up Patch's command". Location: Sélestat, Bas-Rhin with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point stands for the start of the push south from the Selestat region; precision 10 km. Location support: the place is a representative point (inferred value): the source gives only the Selestat region as the start of the push; the date is the planned start; precision 10 km. Commander: Maj. Gen. Jacques Philippe Leclerc commands the division (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 486, note 25; Wikipedia).

The hour is not documented. Event definition: the corps, and with it the 101st Airborne at Bastogne, passes from Hodges' First Army to Patton's Third Army at an undocumented hour of 20 December. The 101st's immediate parent is VIII Corps throughout (operational_control from 18 December, C0553); Third Army's authority over the division is inherited through the corps from the passage, not asserted separately for any earlier day. The question 'who controlled the division at noon on 20 December' is therefore unknown at army level (First Army before the passage, Third Army after it) and scripts/who_controls.py reports it as such. An earlier version of this row was the preferred half of conflict group G016; with the CMH table row reclassified as a table observation (C0563) the group is dissolved. Relationship: VIII Corps operational_control from 18 December; First Allied Airborne Army assigned (table); Third Army attached from 20 December (Green Book), against 17 December in the CMH table, a documented disagreement in which the narrative date is used; 12th Army Group attached through Third Army. Location: Bastogne, the division command post (atlas 19 December; Ardennes p456 for 20 December planning at Bastogne). Coordinates: Wikipedia (en): Bastogne. Event support: moderate (the day is documented; the hour is not, and the table date disagrees). Location support: high (command post at Bastogne for the day).

claims.current_activity: leaves Ninth Army's Roer front for First Army; temporarily attached to XVIII Airborne Corps
claims.notes: Event date: 20 December 1944 (Ardennes p426: Bolling received orders on the night of the 19th to make ready for relief by the 102nd Division, and at noon on 20 December his leading regimental combat team, the 334th, was on the road to Belgium; "Temporarily attached to the XVIII Airborne Corps"; p427: two hours before midnight on 20 December the leading troops entered Marche; the CMH table lists XVIII Airborne Corps and then VII Corps on 20 December). Event definition: Bradley orders the 84th to leave the Ninth Army and come in on Ridgway's flank; the division moves 75 miles from the Geilenkirchen sector to Marche and is the nucleus of the new VII Corps front that Collins assembles from the early morning of the 21st (p426). Relationship (sequence): XVIII Airborne Corps attached from 20 December (narrative) until the VII Corps takes over, between 22 December (last documented XVIII Airborne Corps order, noon, p431) and 23 December (VII Corps officially assumes its front at 1630, p433); VII Corps unspecified_subordination from the CMH table date of 20 December, which is an administrative date, not the date operational control passed; First Army attached; Ninth Army and 12th Army Group assigned; British 21st Army Group attached (CMH table). The immediate parent on the row date is therefore the XVIII Airborne Corps, with First Army above it. Location: Marche is a nearest-later place (inferred): the leading troops entered the town at about 2200 on 20 December (p427), but the division command post is documented there only on 21 December (atlas; p428: the commander set up his command post in Marche on the late afternoon of 21 December, although p429 has word of the Hotton attack reaching the command post in Marche at 0900 that day, an inconsistency in the Green Book), so the headquarters position on the 20th itself is not documented. Coordinates: Wikipedia (en): Marche-en-Famenne. Event support: high (Green Book narrative with times). Location support: moderate (a one-day-later command post; the headquarters place on the date is inferred).

claims.current_activity: Blackcock: attacks from the Wurm to the Juliana Canal; 7th Armoured Division leads on the left at 07:30
claims.notes: Event date: 16 January 1945, 07:30 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 242, 243). Event definition: Operation Blackcock: the front to be attacked by XII Corps runs from the river Wurm, just north of Geilenkirchen, to the Juliana Canal near Maeseyck on the Maas, in a triangle between the Roer and the Maas with its apex at Roermond; General Ritchie decides to start on the left with the 7th Armoured Division and then to follow with attacks by the 52nd Division in the centre and the 43rd Division on the right; delayed by thick fog, the attack begins at 07:30 on 16 January; the only roads of any standing radiate from Sittard to Geilenkirchen, Heinsberg and Roermond (pp. 242-243). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 242: "The front to be attacked by XII Corps ran from the river Wurm, just north of Geilenkirchen, to the Juliana Canal near Maeseyck on the river Maas"; p. 243: "XII Corps commander (General Ritchie) decided to start his attack on the left with 7th Armoured Division and as it progressed to follow with attacks by 52nd Division in the centre and 43rd Division on the right"; "Delayed by thick fog, the attack began at 7.30 a.m. on January the 16th". Location: Sittard, Limburg (new place), on the roads that radiate across the corps front with a precision of 25 km. Location approximate: the point is Sittard, the road centre in the middle of the front named (the Wurm at Geilenkirchen to the Juliana Canal near Maeseyck, about 35 km); the corps headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis gives the corps front from the Wurm near Geilenkirchen to the Juliana Canal near Maeseyck and names Sittard as the road centre of the area (pp. 242-243). Commander: General Ritchie, the XII Corps commander who decided the plan of attack (Ellis, vol. II, p. 243).

claims.current_activity: Blackcock: reaches Susteren on the 17th and has cleared the town by evening after a counter-attack
claims.notes: Event date: 17 January 1945 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 243). Event definition: In Operation Blackcock the division starts on the left on 16 January (the 131st Infantry Brigade group at 07:30 west of the road through Susteren and Linne to Roermond); a second column reaches Susteren on the 17th, part of the town is captured without much difficulty and, after a strong counter-attack is defeated, all has been cleared by evening; troops nearer the Juliana Canal capture Echt by midnight after a sharp fight (p. 243). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 243: "A second column of the 7th Armoured Division moved forward and reached Susteren on the 17th"; "all had been cleared by evening". Location support: Ellis names Susteren as the town reached and cleared (p. 243). claims.current_activity: limited-objective attack at 0300 toward the Roer dams; the 310th Infantry takes Konzen in three hours
claims.notes: Event date: 5 February 1945 (Last Offensive ch. 4 p. 72-75: the 78th Division (Maj. Gen. Edwin P. Parker) jumped off at 0300 on 5 February; in three hours the 310th Infantry cleared thirty-two pillboxes and took the village of Konzen; the 311th Infantry fought for Kesternich; the division had passed to the operational control of V Corps on 2 February). Event definition: the division opens the attack of V Corps toward the Roer dams; the row is the first day of the attack and the village its first objective. Relationship: V Corps operational_control (from 2 Feb 45, narrative); XVIII Airborne Corps unspecified_subordination (from 3 Feb 45 to 11 Feb 45, CMH table); First Army assigned (from 2 Feb 45, CMH table); 12th Army Group assigned (from 9 Nov 44, CMH table). The table entries start on the first row of the unbroken run (convention V-013). The CMH table has a single corps column and does not say assigned or attached for a corps. claims.current_activity: Veritable: takes the Brandenberg hill by 14:00; through the Siegfried defences by 02:00 on the 9th
claims.notes: Event date: 8 February 1945 (to 14:00 and 02:00 on the 9th) (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 258, 259). Event definition: On 8 February the division has the task of making good the northern half of the Reichswald and in particular the Brandenberg and Stoppelberg features; it leads with the 71st Brigade for the Brandenberg, the ground becomes a quagmire and all vehicles except a few Churchills are bogged, but by two o'clock the infantry are on the Brandenberg hill and mopping up the German 84th Division; the 160th Brigade, starting from Groesbeek and slowed by congestion, attacks late in the day and by 02:00 on the 9th has its leading units through the Siegfried defences (pp. 258-259). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 482: "On 15 February the 3rd Canadian Division took over the 15th Division's front, at the same time reverting under the command of the 2nd Canadian Corps"; p. 484: "The failure to drive the enemy from Moyland Wood was seriously delaying the 2nd Canadian Corps". Location: Cleve (Kleve), North Rhine-Westphalia (existing place PL0578) with a precision of 25 km. Location approximate: the point is Cleve, standing for the corps sector; it is not a headquarters position. Location support: Stacey places the 3rd Division front between the inter-corps boundary and the flooded Rhine flats near Moyland and the 2nd Division 4th Brigade in the Cleve area (pp. 482-484); the corps headquarters place is not stated. Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

claims.current_activity: Plunder: comes into action on the night of 26 March and captures Megchelen (Ellis: Mechelen) early on the 28th
claims.notes: Event date: 28 March 1945, early (Ellis, vol. II, p. 293). Event definition: On the night of 26-27 March the division comes into action in the XXX Corps bridgehead at Rees and goes on to capture Mechelen early on 28 March, by which time most of the 3rd Canadian Division is across the Rhine and advancing west to take Emmerich and the 51st Division has secured Isselburg (Ellis, vol. II, p. 293); the village named Mechelen is the Dutch village of Megchelen, just over the Dutch frontier, which a local-history foundation records as entered by part of the Wessex Division on the morning of 28 March, after it had fought its way through Millingen on 26-27 March (Opdat Wij Niet Vergeten). Event support: two source families (Ellis, the British official history, and a Dutch local-history foundation, Opdat Wij Niet Vergeten). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 293-295: "That night the 43rd Division came into action and went on to capture Mechelen early on the 28th"; "the 51st Division had secured Isselburg"; Opdat Wij Niet Vergeten, "Megchelen bevrijd": "In de ochtend van 28 maart glipt een deel van de Wessex Divisie langs de Duitse flank en dringt, vlak over de Nederlandse grens, Megchelen binnen"; "Megchelen in de Tweede Wereldoorlog": "Op de ochtend van 28 maart 1945 bereikten Britse troepen Megchelen". Location: Megchelen, Gelderland (new place), the village just over the Dutch frontier with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the village of Megchelen; the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Mechelen between the Rhine bridgehead at Rees, Isselburg and Emmerich (p. 293); the local-history pages place the 43rd Division in Megchelen on the morning of 28 March. Commander: Maj.-Gen. G. I. Thomas, commanding the 43rd (Wessex) Division (Ellis, vol. II, p. 375). Context: Review (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026; the place name is an identification): Ellis spells the village Mechelen, which is the Dutch Megchelen; Ellis names it once, on p. 293. The context (the 43rd Division advancing from Rees through Millingen towards Isselburg, Emmerich on the left) and the local-history pages that give Megchelen on 28 March place it at Megchelen. No other place of that name lies on the road from the Rhine bridgehead at Rees to Isselburg and Emmerich. The row is kept at 0.7 because the day and the unit are in Ellis and the village is confirmed by the second source. The earlier operational_control relation to XXII Corps (CR0477) is closed at 1 April 1945 (inferred_from_next_claim); see the Review note on it. Review (26 October 2026, found while adding this row): the CMH table row of 4 Apr 45 lists "XIV" in the Corps column and the Combat Chronicle lists XIX Corps until 8 April and XVI Corps from 9 April; no relation to XIV Corps is recorded, and the table-based relation to XIX Corps is made from 2 April to 3 April only (the day before the row that no longer lists it). The Green Book (ch. 16 p. 366) says that the XIX Corps commander grouped the 95th Division, the 8th Armored Division and the 15th Cavalry Group on 7 April into Task Force Twaddle under the 95th Division commander and that General Simpson transferred its operational control to the XVI Corps; the table lists XVI Corps from 9 April. Event definition: The 53rd Division comes up, crosses the Weser south of Verden (still firmly held by the enemy) and attacks the German 2nd Naval Division at Rethem, where a main road to Hamburg crosses the Aller; XII Corps fails to capture Rethem on 11 April, but the enemy withdraws that night and an outflanking operation over an unguarded crossing five miles downstream helps the division to gain the high ground north of the town; the division, with the 4th Armoured Brigade, then turns north-west to capture the high ground north of Verden and the town itself; the ground is strongly defended, with German Marines counter-attacking at night, and Verden is not secured till 17 April (pp. 306 and 310). claims.current_activity: a patrol of the 273d Infantry crosses the Elbe by boat near Strehla and meets Soviet soldiers, the first contact
claims.notes: Event date: 25 April 1945 (Last Offensive ch. 19 p. 450-453: Lt. Kotzebue's patrol went beyond the Mulde to Kuehren and, on the morning of 25 April, east through Dahlen to the Elbe a few hundred yards north of Strehla, where five of his men rowed across and met Soviet soldiers of the 175th Regiment; his message was signed at 1330; Lt. Robertson's patrol met Soviet soldiers at the Torgau bridge about forty-five minutes later; Wikipedia, Elbe Day: the first documented contact took place on the morning of 25 April near Strehla, the best-known meeting later that day at Torgau). Event definition: the first contact between American and Soviet forces, made by a patrol of the division's 273d Infantry; the division commander met the Soviet commander at Torgau at 1600 on 26 April (p. 456). The row is the place of the contact, not the headquarters. Relationship: V Corps unspecified_subordination (from 7 Feb 45 to 27 Apr 45, CMH table); First Army assigned (from 7 Feb 45, CMH table); 12th Army Group assigned (from 18 Jan 45, CMH table). The table entries start on the first row of the unbroken run (convention V-013). The CMH table has a single corps column and does not say assigned or attached for a corps. The earlier unspecified_subordination relation to V Corps (CR0438) is closed at 27 April 1945 (assignment_table); see the Review note on it. Location: Strehla on the Elbe, the town standing for the crossing point a few hundred yards to its north; the second meeting, at the Torgau bridge (about 28 km down the river), is named in the notes only. Coordinates: Wikipedia (en): Strehla. Event support: strong (the Green Book and Wikipedia agree on the day and on Strehla). Location support: good (named town; the Green Book puts the crossing at the Elbe a few hundred yards north of it). Context: Wikipedia puts the first contact "on the morning of 25 April"; the Green Book (p. 450-452) has the patrol set out early and the message signed at 1330, and says that the second meeting, Robertson's at Torgau, came about 45 minutes after Craig's contact (p. 454); the hour of the first contact is not stated in the passages read, so no time is recorded. Context (27 October 2026, spot check): the regimental history of the 273d Infantry (R584) puts Kotzebue's patrol at Leckwitz near Strehla at 1130 on 25 April, Robertson's patrol on the Torgau bridge at 1600 and Craig's patrol at Clanzschwitz at 1645, and gives the first patrol as 11 men (a photograph caption says 36) where the Green Book says Kotzebue and five men; the day and the place agree.

Event support: one source family (FMS, German postwar manuscripts). Location: Amersfoort, Utrecht (place PL3537) with a precision of 25 km.
